gonna be tricky to fix...

your code is fine.   the whole idea of "LATERAL" is that ....the cartesian product searcher thing also has to learn how to join laterally :)    there was an unfortunate issue where the test suite didn't have cartesian linting turned on for our lateral tests.

I know it may be a lot of work and / or a breaking change, but a better solution could be to introduce a `lateraljoin()` operator and deprecate `lateral()`.

1. That may make solving the issue at hand easier
2. It will help with https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/issues/5133 ('Add APPLY operator support for mssql') for instance by providing a "general" solution for all databases
3. We do not have to use an awkward construct such as `join(..., true())` 

Thanks

In the meantime, is there a way to suppress this warning (it is clogging our logs), or do you think there is a way to re-write the query differently not to trigger the cartesian product searcher  - I have already tried a couple things but they did not work :(

Thanks

the from linting can be turned off quite simply by passing enable_from_linting=False to create_engine:

https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/14/core/engines.html?highlight=from%20linting#sqlalchemy.create_engine.params.enable_from_linting

also this is hard to fix not because of the API, it's hard because I have to emulate the geometry of "lateral" in the compiler, but the good news is that math and recursion still work so a fix is coming up shortly

**Mike Bayer** has proposed a fix for this issue in the **master** branch:

**Track a second from_linter for lateral subqueries** https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/2536

oh also with this fix (or if you set the option off for now) you should not have to join() on true(), this works:

    query = select(a, b, c)

output:

```sql
SELECT anon_1.id, anon_1.value, anon_2.value AS value_1, anon_3.value AS value_2 
FROM (SELECT "A".id AS id, "A".value AS value 
FROM "A") AS anon_1, LATERAL (SELECT "B".value AS value 
FROM "B" 
WHERE anon_1.id = "B".id_a ORDER BY "B".value 
 LIMIT %(param_1)s) AS anon_2, LATERAL (SELECT "C".value AS value 
FROM "C" 
WHERE anon_1.id = "C".id_a ORDER BY "C".value 
 LIMIT %(param_2)s) AS anon_3

```
LATERAL is SQL standard, and it does not require JOIN, so we do that
I will try that and also `enable_from_linting` flag until next release. Thanks!

> Thanks

Since that is a classical python warning, you could setup a warning filter for that emissing. https://docs.python.org/3/library/warnings.html

Something like this should work
```py
import warnings
warnings.simplefilter("ignore:SELECT statement has a cartesian product.*:SAWarning")
```

Thanks for the idea @CaselIT !

This is what worked for me (I was able to pinpoint the fix on only the very query that was at fault):
```        
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.filterwarnings(
        "ignore", "SELECT statement has a cartesian product.*", SAWarning
    )
    ...
```

why?    I'm not following?    what's "outer LATERAL" ?

I went for the context manager version because only one of my queries was concerned, and I did not want to broadly suppress that message as it is useful and relevant in other queries.

issue.title: query.join is ignoring Table objects as targets

labels.name: regression
labels.description: something worked and was broken by a change

issue.body:
**Describe the bug**
A regular inner join is compiled as a cartesian join.

**Expected behavior**
This should produce a regular left-outer join between tables 1 and 2, and an (inner) join between tables 1 and 3. This works properly in version 1.3.23. The error observed above was seen in 1.4.0b2.

**To Reproduce**

Using version 1.4.0b2,

```
query = (
    session
    .query(<columns from table1>) 
    .outerjoin(table3, <table1 and table3 join condition>)
    .join(table2, <table1 and table2 join condition>)
    .filter(<some more conditions>)
)
```

**Error**

```
.../sqlalchemy/sql/compiler.py:357: SAWarning: SELECT statement has a cartesian product between FROM element(s) "TABLE1" and FROM element "TABLE2".  Apply join condition(s) between each element to resolve.
    util.warn(message)
```

Note that the warning warns about the table joined using ``.join`` and not the table joined in the ``.outerjoin``.

The warning is not a mistake, in the final results we really do see the result of a cartesian join instead of a proper inner join.

**Versions.**
 - OS: Ubuntu (recent, not sure the exact version)
 - Python: 3.9
 - SQLAlchemy: 1.4.0b2
 - Database: MSSQL
 - DBAPI: FreeTDS

**Additional context**
Works properly in 1.3.23

**Have a nice day!**

issue.title: Using posgresql.ARRAY.overlap() in a multiple join scenario gives a cartesian product warning

labels.name: great mcve
labels.description: An issue with a great mcve

issue.body:
### Describe the bug

A query that joins three entities on `ARRAY.overlap` conditions triggers a cartesian product warning despite the correct SQL being emitted.

### To Reproduce

```python
import sqlalchemy as sa
from sqlalchemy.dialects import postgresql
from sqlalchemy.ext.declarative import declarative_base
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session, aliased


Base = declarative_base()


class Foo(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'foo'

    id = sa.Column(sa.Integer, primary_key=True, autoincrement=True)
    ancestors_ids = sa.Column(postgresql.ARRAY(sa.Integer), nullable=False, server_default='{}')
    is_bar = sa.Column(sa.Boolean, nullable=False)


engine = sa.create_engine('postgresql://user:pass@localhost:5432/db')
# engine.execute('drop table foo;')
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
session = Session(engine)

ancestor = aliased(Foo, name='ancestor')
descendant = aliased(Foo, name='descendant')
qs = (
    session
    .query(Foo)
    .with_entities(
        Foo.id,
        Foo.is_bar,
        sa.func.bool_or(ancestor.is_bar).label('ancestor_is_bar'),
        sa.func.bool_or(descendant.is_bar).label('descendant_is_bar'),
    )
    .join(
        ancestor,
        sa.and_(
            Foo.ancestors_ids.overlap(postgresql.array((ancestor.id,))),
            ancestor.is_bar.is_(True),
        ),
        isouter=True,
    )
    .join(
        descendant,
        sa.and_(
            descendant.ancestors_ids.overlap(postgresql.array((Foo.id,))),
            descendant.is_bar.is_(True),
        ),
        isouter=True,
    )
    .group_by(
        Foo.id,
        Foo.is_bar,
    )
)
print(qs)

# SELECT
#     foo.id AS foo_id,
#     foo.is_bar AS foo_is_bar,
#     bool_or(ancestor.is_bar) AS ancestor_is_bar,
#     bool_or(descendant.is_bar) AS descendant_is_bar
# FROM foo
#     LEFT OUTER JOIN foo AS ancestor
#         ON foo.ancestors_ids && ARRAY[ancestor.id] AND ancestor.is_bar IS true
#     LEFT OUTER JOIN foo AS descendant
#         ON descendant.ancestors_ids && ARRAY[foo.id] AND descendant.is_bar IS true
# GROUP BY
#     foo.id,
#     foo.is_bar

print(qs.all())
```


### Error

SAWarning: SELECT statement has a cartesian product between FROM element(s) "ancestor", "foo" and FROM element "descendant".  Apply join condition(s) between each element to resolve.

>    print(qs.all())



### Versions

- OS: Arch Linux 5.4 (Manjaro)
- Python: 3.9.6
- SQLAlchemy: 1.4.22
- Database: Postgresql 13.3
- DBAPI: psycopg2-binary 2.9.1

### Additional context

I've read https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/issues/5924 as it seemed correlated but after some testing I don't think it is, as this issue was particular to the type of `JOIN` used.

Here, changing the join type from `isouter=True` to `isouter=False` still triggers the warning. Moreover, replacing the `ancestors_ids` array column on `Foo` by a `parent_id` integer column and then replacing the `.overlap` join conditions by a simple `id`/`parent_id` equality doesn't trigger the warning. This seems to indicate that the problem comes specifically from using `.overlap` in a multiple join scenario and not from the join types themselves.

Finally, I don't know if that helps but while trying to ignore the warnings in pytest I ran into a bit of a quirk: the warning's message changes with every execution (assuming the .pyc have been recreated):
`SELECT statement has a cartesian product between FROM element(s) "foo", "ancestor" and FROM element "descendant"`
`SELECT statement has a cartesian product between FROM element(s) "descendant" and FROM element "ancestor"`
`SELECT statement has a cartesian product between FROM element(s) "descendant" and FROM element "foo"`
After a good dozen tries I got these three distinct messages which all point to the second join (the one with descendant) being the triggering point.
